power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: Background: The Conversation Questionnaire (CQ) assesses everyday conversational difficulties through items developed with autistic adults.
We translated the CQ into German and examined whether its psychometric properties reproduced the original findings.
Methods: Translation, author consultation, and cognitive debriefing with 15 self-reported autistic adults preceded validation in 185 native German-speaking adults.
Participants reported an autism diagnosis (diagnosed), suspected or self-identified autism (suspected), or neither.
We reanalyzed the original data (n = 266) to provide comparable benchmarks.
We approximated the original broader cognitive-ability comparison with nonverbal matrix reasoning and extended validation to the recall of childhood coordination difficulties.
Results: Item response theory modeling closely reproduced two dimensions: difficulty knowing what to say (15 items) and misunderstandings or behaviors affecting conversation (21 items).
Only two of 36 items showed shifted loadings, while reliability remained high for both dimensions (.94 and .90, respectively).
As in the reanalyzed original data, both dimensions distinguished the diagnosed and neither groups.
The suspected group had intermediate average scores, with overlapping individual scores across groups.

Correlations with the CQ's Core Language Difficulties and Negative Interaction Style control subscales were stronger for the second dimension, while correlations with reasoning performance were near zero.
Extending the original validation, both dimensions correlated strongly with recalled childhood coordination difficulties (r = .64-.71).
Conclusion: These findings support the German CQ as a reliable, community-informed measure for characterizing conversational experiences among autistic and non-autistic German-speaking adults.
Our findings also connect conversational experiences to childhood coordination abilities, showing the questionnaire's relevance to broader neurodevelopmental research.
Why is this an important issue?
Conversation can be demanding even when others do not notice the effort involved.
The Conversation Questionnaire (CQ) was developed in cooperation with autistic adults with a focus on everyday, non-pathologizing statements.
The German version makes this measure available to researchers in German-speaking countries.
It will allow cross-cultural and international comparisons and contribute to the study of associations between behavioral and brain processes.
We translated the CQ and examined whether German responses reproduced the question groupings, score consistency, and autism-status patterns reported in the original study.
Two translators and the first author developed the German wording, consulted the original author, and sought feedback from 15 self-reported autistic adults.
We then studied 185 native Germanspeaking adults who reported an autism diagnosis (diagnosed), suspected or self-identified autism (suspected), or neither.
We reanalyzed data from 266 participants in the original Englishlanguage study to compare the German findings with the original results.

We compared scores between groups and examined associations with the CQ's control subscales, Core Language Difficulties and Negative Interaction Style, as well as performance on visual pattern puzzles, recalled childhood coordination difficulties, sex assigned at birth, age, and education.
The German CQ largely reproduced the published question groupings and high score consistency.
Scores differed significantly across reported autism-status groups: the diagnosed group had the highest scores and the suspected group intermediate scores.
Scores correlated more strongly with Core Language Difficulties than Negative Interaction Style and showed little association with visual pattern reasoning.
Adults who recalled more childhood coordination difficulties reported significantly greater conversational difficulties.

The coordination findings extend earlier English-language research to the two aspects of conversation measured by the German CQ.
Associations with Core Language Difficulties and Negative Interaction Style followed the original pattern but were somewhat stronger here.
